newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FEATURE - Thieves flog booty at Lisbon market.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Thieves flog booty at Lisbon market.

text.p: Under cover of darkness Lisbon's thieves, many of them drug addicts, sell their booty to the highest bidder at a downtown market popular with tourists.
At dawn the Thief's Market is the scene of an illicit trade in goods ranging from car radios to silver cutlery stolen at night from the cars and homes of law-abiding citizens.

The Thief's Market, which according to historical accounts was named after a woman trader who was nicknamed Thief, has been based in the old Sao Vicente quarter of central Lisbon since early last century.
One man living in an insecure neighbourhood said he returned regularly to the market in the early hours when it opened on a Tuesday or Saturday to track down the radio stolen from his car.
Sometimes he found it and would pay a rockbottom price to recover it.
A reporter witnessed several transactions involving young male drug addicts selling stolen car radios at the market.
Surreptitiously, they opened plastic bags carrying their haul. Passers-by quickly gathered round and the haggling began.
"10,000 escudos ($60) for a Sony," said the moustachioed addict, whose hand bore a tattoo with the words "The Doors."
"I'll give you 7,000," said a man in a track suit with a rucksack on his back.
"No. It's a Sony. It's a good radio. 8,000 escudos," replied the seller, who had a friend standing by to mind his goods while he negotiated.
The deal was transacted at 7,500 escudos and the vendor brought out another radio from his bag, snatched during a long night's work from a vehicle parked somewhere in Lisbon.
And the dealing went on.
Another man, selling a vast silver cutlery set, was surrounded by a crowd of buyers, some of whom were licensed market traders and others respectable citizens in suits.
This was a good prize and it did not take long before he sold it for a bargain 10,000 escudos.
Of course it was hard to tell in the dark if the cutlery was really silver. And nobody could be sure that the car radios worked.
RISKS FOR BUYERS AND SELLERS ALIKE
There are no guarantees for goods sold at this market.
Buying is as much of a gamble as selling.
The risk for the buyer is that the produce is not genuine or is broken.
The risk for the seller of stolen goods is that the police could strike at any moment.
During the reporter's visit, plainclothes police arrested three youths caught selling CD-ROMs with pirated software.
Customers and traders jeered as police led them away.
"The police should leave us alone," said Luis, an unlicensed market trader.
"We provide things people want cheaply. We're doing a service," he said.
The victims of the thefts would disagree.
Portugal is a major European transhipment point for drugs from Asia and South America. The addicts use the proceeds of their stolen goods to feed their habit.
Many of the sellers at the market are legitimate business people who have licences to ply their trade.
Some Lisbon residents who do not have licences say they go to the market to sell their unwanted junk. They trade as quickly and early as they can in order to evade the police.
Transactions halt as a police car stops briefly. An officer chats to a trader before driving off.
The market is a place to buy all kinds of goods -- from old books and collector's coins to fruit and vegetables and used sunglasses, compact discs and clothes.
By the time dawn breaks the market has turned into a respectable forum and the thieves have slipped away.
